Let
\[
z=\frac{x}{1+x}=x(1+x)^{-1},\qquad u=y-z.
\]
This is well-defined because \(x\) is nilpotent, so \(1+x\) is invertible. The center is
\[
\boxed{
Z(R_m)=k\left[z^3,\ u^3,\ z^{3m}u,\ z^{3m}u^2\right]
}
\]
where \(z=x(1+x)^{-1}\) and \(u=y-x(1+x)^{-1}\). Since \(z^{3m}=x^{3m}\), equivalently
\[
\boxed{
Z(R_m)=k\left[
\left(\frac{x}{1+x}\right)^3,\ 
\left(y-\frac{x}{1+x}\right)^3,\ 
x^{3m}y,\ 
x^{3m}y^2
\right].
}
\]

Here is the derivation.

Put \(a=1-\omega\). From
\[
(1+ax)yx=\omega xy+ax^2
\]
and the invertibility of \(1+ax\), we get
\[
yx=\frac{\omega x}{1+ax}y+\frac{ax^2}{1+ax}.
\]
Now set
\[
z=\frac{x}{1+x}.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{z}{1-z}=x,
\]
so changing from \(x\) to \(z\) is an invertible change of generator. A direct calculation gives
\[
\sigma(z)=\omega z,
\]
and with \(u=y-z\), the relation becomes
\[
uz=\omega zu.
\]
Also \(z^{3m+1}=0\). Thus
\[
R_m\cong k[z]/(z^{3m+1})[u;\sigma],
\qquad \sigma(z)=\omega z,
\]
so every element has a unique form
\[
\sum_{j\ge 0} f_j(z)u^j,
\qquad f_j(z)\in k[z]/(z^{3m+1}).
\]

Now impose centrality. Commuting with \(u\) gives
\[
f_j(z)=f_j(\omega z),
\]
so each \(f_j\) is a polynomial in \(z^3\). Commuting with \(z\) gives
\[
z f_j(z)u^j=\omega^j z f_j(z)u^j.
\]
If \(3\mid j\), this imposes no new condition. If \(3\nmid j\), then \(zf_j(z)=0\), hence
\[
f_j(z)\in k z^{3m}.
\]
Because \(z^{3m}\) itself is fixed by \(\sigma\), the central elements are exactly finite sums of the form
\[
P(z^3,u^3)+\alpha(z^{3m}u)Q(u^3)+\beta(z^{3m}u^2)Q'(u^3),
\]
which is precisely the subalgebra
\[
k[z^3,u^3,z^{3m}u,z^{3m}u^2].
\]

Returning to \(x,y\), this is
\[
\boxed{
Z(R_m)=k\left[
\left(\frac{x}{1+x}\right)^3,\ 
\left(y-\frac{x}{1+x}\right)^3,\ 
x^{3m}y,\ 
x^{3m}y^2
\right].
}
\]
